concept.name: OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code Flow
concept.title: OAuth: delegated access without sharing a password
concept.definition: OAuth lets a user authorize one application to call another service on their behalf. The client receives a limited access token instead of the user's password.
concept.problem: An application needs delegated access to a user's data without collecting the user's credentials or receiving unlimited permission.

goals: separate user-facing consent from backend token exchange

nodes.label: User
nodes.caption: owns the data
nodes.description: The resource owner deciding whether the client application may access protected data.

nodes.label: Client App
nodes.caption: requests delegated access
nodes.description: The product asking for limited access to another service on the user's behalf.

nodes.label: Login and Consent
nodes.caption: user-facing decision
nodes.description: The authorization server verifies the user and shows which permissions the client requests.

nodes.label: Authorization Server
nodes.caption: issues grants and tokens
nodes.description: The trusted system that runs consent, validates the client, and issues short-lived credentials.

nodes.label: Access Token
nodes.caption: limited delegated credential
nodes.description: A time-limited credential with specific scopes. It is for API authorization and is not the user's password.

nodes.label: Resource Server
nodes.caption: the protected API
nodes.description: The API that validates the access token and enforces its scopes before returning protected data.

nodes.label: Protected Data
nodes.caption: the permitted result
nodes.description: Only the data and actions permitted by the access token's scopes should be available.

groups.label: Authorization Boundary
groups.description: The trusted service where the user signs in, sees requested scopes, and grants access.

groups.label: Protected API Boundary
groups.description: The service that validates access tokens and applies scope checks to protected data.

chapters.title: The client requests access
chapters.explanation: The user starts a connection in the client app. The client redirects the browser to the trusted authorization server with requested scopes.
takeaways: The authorization server owns the login surface

chapters.title: The user reviews and approves
chapters.explanation: The authorization server authenticates the user and presents the requested permissions. The user can approve or reject them.
takeaways: Consent should name the requested access
The user's password stays with the authorization server

chapters.title: A one-time code returns
chapters.explanation: After approval, the browser returns to the client with a short-lived authorization code. The code is not the API credential.

chapters.title: The backend exchanges the code
chapters.explanation: The client backend sends the code to the authorization server through a direct channel and receives a limited access token.
takeaways: The token exchange belongs on a trusted backend
Access tokens need short lifetimes and narrow scopes

chapters.title: The client calls the protected API
chapters.explanation: The client presents the access token to the resource server. The API validates it, enforces scopes, and returns only the permitted data.

roleRelevance.title: Why this matters for a Product Manager
points: Design requested scopes as a product trust decision, not only an engineering setting.
Make the redirect and consent journey understandable before asking the user to approve.
Treat reconnect, expiry, revocation, and denied consent as explicit product states.
Use OpenID Connect when the product also needs a standardized sign-in identity layer.

contextCards.title: Authorization, not identity
points: OAuth answers what a client may access.
OAuth alone does not standardize who signed in.
OpenID Connect adds identity claims on top of OAuth.

contextCards.title: Token safety
points: Use short-lived, narrowly scoped access tokens.
Keep backend exchanges out of browser-visible secrets.
Support revocation and clear reconnection flows.

contextCards.title: User experience states
points: Explain why each permission is needed.
Handle rejected consent without a dead end.
Show when access expires or must be reauthorized.
